title: Part 1, Chapter 47
paragraphs: About the strange way Don Quixote of La Mancha was carried off under enchantment, with other remarkable incidents

When Don Quixote found himself caged and hoisted onto the cart like this, he said, "I have read many serious histories of knights-errant, but never yet have I read, seen, or heard of their carrying off enchanted knights-errant in this fashion, or at the slow pace these lazy, sluggish beasts promise. They always take them through the air with marvellous swiftness, wrapped in a thick dark cloud, or on a chariot of fire, or perhaps on some hippogriff or other beast of the kind. But to carry me off like this on an ox-cart — by God, it puzzles me. Perhaps the chivalry and enchantments of our day take a different course from those of times gone by. And it may be too that, as I am a new knight in the world, the first to revive the long-forgotten calling of knight-adventurers, they have newly invented other kinds of enchantments and other ways of carrying off the enchanted. What do you make of it, Sancho my son?"

"I don't know what to make of it," Sancho answered, "not being as well read as your worship in chivalric writings; but for all that I'll venture to say and swear that these apparitions hovering around us are not quite Catholic."

"Catholic!" said Don Quixote. "Good heavens, how can they be Catholic when they're all devils in fantastic shapes, come here to do this and reduce me to this state? And if you want proof, touch them, feel them, and you'll find they have only bodies of air, no substance except in appearance."

"By God, master," Sancho returned, "I've already touched them, and that devil bustling about over there has firm flesh, and a property quite different from what I've heard tell of devils. By all accounts they all smell of brimstone and other bad smells; but this one smells of amber half a league off." Sancho was speaking of Don Fernando, who, as a gentleman of his rank, was very likely perfumed as Sancho said.

"Don't marvel at that, Sancho my friend," said Don Quixote. "Let me tell you: devils are cunning, and even if they carry scents about them, they themselves have no smell, because they're spirits; or if they do have a smell, it can't be of anything sweet but of something foul and stinking. The reason is that, since they carry hell with them wherever they go and can get no relief from their torments, and since a sweet smell gives pleasure and enjoyment, it's impossible they should smell sweet. If this devil you speak of seems to you to smell of amber, either you're deceiving yourself, or he's trying to deceive you by making you fancy he's not a devil."

Such was the conversation between master and man. Don Fernando and Cardenio, worried that Sancho might fully see through their scheme — towards which he had already gone some way — resolved to hasten their departure. Calling the landlord aside, they ordered him to saddle Rocinante and put the pack-saddle on Sancho's ass, which he did with great speed. Meanwhile the curate had arranged with the officers that they should accompany them as far as his village, he paying them so much a day. Cardenio hung the buckler on one side of the bow of Rocinante's saddle and the basin on the other, and by signs ordered Sancho to mount his ass and take Rocinante's bridle. At each side of the cart he placed two officers with their muskets. But before the cart was set in motion, the landlady, her daughter, and Maritornes came out to bid Don Quixote farewell, pretending to weep with grief at his misfortune. To them Don Quixote said:

"Weep not, good ladies, for all these mishaps are the lot of those who follow the profession I profess. If such setbacks did not befall me I should not count myself a famous knight-errant, for such things never happen to knights of little renown and fame, because no one in the world gives them a thought. They happen to valiant knights, for these are envied for their virtue and valour by many princes and other knights, who plot the destruction of the worthy by base means. Nevertheless, virtue is in itself so mighty that, in spite of all the magic that Zoroaster, its first inventor, knew, she will come victorious out of every trial and shed her light upon the earth as the sun does upon the heavens. Forgive me, fair ladies, if through inadvertence I have in any way offended you, for intentionally and knowingly I have never offended anyone. Pray to God that He deliver me from this captivity to which some malevolent enchanter has consigned me; and should I find myself freed, the favours you have shown me in this castle shall be held in memory by me, that I may acknowledge, recognise, and repay them as they deserve."

While this was passing between the ladies of the castle and Don Quixote, the curate and the barber said goodbye to Don Fernando and his companions, to the captain, his brother, and the ladies — now all made happy — and especially to Dorothea and Luscinda. They all embraced and promised to let one another know how things went, and Don Fernando told the curate where to write to him to report what became of Don Quixote, assuring him that nothing could give him more pleasure than to hear of it; he himself, in turn, would send word of everything he thought the curate would like to know — his marriage, Zoraida's baptism, Don Luis's situation, and Luscinda's return home. The curate promised to comply with the request carefully, and they embraced once more and renewed their promises.

The landlord went up to the curate and handed him some papers, saying he had found them in the lining of the valise in which the novel of "The Ill-advised Curiosity" had been found, and that the curate could take them all since their owner had not returned; he could not read them himself. The curate thanked him, and on opening them saw at the beginning of the manuscript the words "Novel of Rinconete and Cortadillo," by which he could tell it was a novel. Since "The Ill-advised Curiosity" had been good, he concluded this one would be too, since they were probably by the same author; so he kept it, intending to read it when he had the chance. He then mounted up, and his friend the barber did the same — both masked, so Don Quixote wouldn't recognise them — and they set out following behind the cart. The order of march was this: first went the cart with the owner leading it; on each side marched the officers of the Brotherhood, as already mentioned, with their muskets; then came Sancho Panza on his ass, leading Rocinante by the bridle; and bringing up the rear were the curate and the barber on their stout mules, faces covered as said, with a grave and serious bearing, measuring their pace to the slow steps of the oxen. Don Quixote sat in the cage with his hands tied and his feet stretched out, leaning against the bars, as silent and patient as a stone statue rather than a man of flesh. Going slowly and silently they made perhaps two leagues until they reached a valley which the carter thought a good place to rest and feed his oxen. He said as much to the curate, but the barber thought they should push on a little farther, because on the other side of a hill that appeared close by he knew of a valley with more and better grass. His advice was taken, and they continued on.

Just then the curate, glancing back, saw six or seven mounted men coming up behind, well outfitted and equipped, who soon caught up with them, for they were travelling not at the sluggish pace of oxen but like men riding canons' mules, in a hurry to take their noontide rest as soon as possible at the inn that was in sight not a league off. The quick travellers met up with the slow ones, and courteous greetings were exchanged. One of the newcomers, who was in fact a canon of Toledo and master of the others with him, observed the orderly procession — the cart, the officers, Sancho, Rocinante, the curate and the barber, and above all Don Quixote caged and confined — and could not help asking what was meant by carrying the man in that fashion, though, from the officers' badges, he already concluded he must be some desperate highwayman or other criminal whose punishment fell within the Holy Brotherhood's jurisdiction. One of the officers to whom he put the question replied, "Let the gentleman himself tell you the meaning of his going this way, señor, because we don't know."

Don Quixote overheard the conversation and said, "Perhaps, gentlemen, you are versed and learned in matters of errant chivalry? If so, I'll tell you my misfortunes; if not, there's no point in my troubling myself to relate them." But here the curate and the barber, seeing the travellers were in conversation with Don Quixote, came forward, ready to answer in such a way as to keep their scheme from being discovered.

Replying to Don Quixote, the canon said, "To tell the truth, brother, I know more about books of chivalry than I do about Villalpando's elements of logic; so if that's all, you may safely tell me whatever you please."

"In God's name, then, señor," replied Don Quixote, "if that's so, I'll have you know that I am held enchanted in this cage by the envy and treachery of wicked enchanters, since virtue is more persecuted by the wicked than loved by the good. I am a knight-errant — and not one of those whose names Fame never thought of immortalising, but of those who, in defiance and despite of envy itself, and all the magicians that Persia, or Brahmans that India, or Gymnosophists that Ethiopia ever produced, will set their names in the temple of immortality, to serve as examples and patterns for ages to come, that knights-errant may see the footsteps in which they must tread to reach the summit and crowning point of honour in arms."

"What Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha says," observed the curate, "is the truth. He goes enchanted in this cart, not for any fault or sin of his, but because of the malice of those to whom virtue is odious and valour hateful. This, señor, is the Knight of the Rueful Countenance — if you've ever heard him named — whose valiant achievements and mighty deeds shall be written on lasting brass and imperishable marble, despite all the efforts of envy to obscure them and malice to hide them."

When the canon heard both the prisoner and the man who was at liberty speaking in this way, he was ready to cross himself in astonishment, and could not make out what was happening; all his attendants were in the same state of amazement.

At this point Sancho Panza, who had drawn near to hear the conversation, said, to make matters plain, "Well, sirs, you can like it or not, but the fact is, my master Don Quixote is just about as enchanted as my mother. He's in his full senses; he eats and he drinks and he answers nature's calls like other men, and as he did yesterday before they caged him. If that's the case, what do they mean by trying to make me believe he's enchanted? I've heard many a one say that enchanted people don't eat, sleep, or talk — and my master, if you don't stop him, will talk more than thirty lawyers." Then turning to the curate he exclaimed, "Ah, señor curate, señor curate! Do you think I don't know you? Do you think I can't guess what these new enchantments are about? Well, I can tell you I do know you, no matter how covered your face is, and I'm on to you, however much you hide your tricks. In the end, where envy reigns, virtue can't live, and where there's stinginess there can be no generosity. Curse the devil! If it hadn't been for your worship, my master would have been married to Princess Micomicona by now, and I'd be a count at least — for no less was to be expected, as much from the goodness of my master, him of the Rueful Countenance, as from the greatness of my services. But I see now how true it is what they say in these parts, that the wheel of fortune turns faster than a mill-wheel, and those who were up yesterday are down today. I'm sorry for my wife and children; when they could reasonably have hoped to see their father come back a governor or viceroy of some island or kingdom, they'll see him come home a stable-hand. I'm saying all this, señor curate, only to urge your paternity to take to your conscience this ill-treatment of my master, and to be careful that God doesn't call you to account in the next life for making him a prisoner this way, and charge against you all the rescues and good deeds my lord Don Quixote leaves undone while he's shut up."

"Trim those wicks!" exclaimed the barber at this. "So you're of the same fraternity as your master, are you, Sancho? By God, I'm starting to see you'll have to keep him company in the cage and be enchanted like him for having caught some of his humour and chivalry. It was an evil hour you let yourself be got with child by his promises, and that island you long for so much wormed its way into your head."

"I'm not with child by anyone," Sancho returned, "nor am I a man to let himself be got with child, not by the King himself. I may be poor, but I'm an old Christian, and I owe nothing to nobody; and if I long for an island, other people long for worse. Each of us is the son of his own works; and being a man I may come to be pope, never mind governor of an island — especially as my master may win so many that he won't know whom to give them to. Mind how you talk, master barber; for shaving isn't everything, and there's some difference between one Peter and another. I say this because we all know one another, and it won't do to throw false dice with me; and as for my master's enchantment, God knows the truth — leave it alone; it only gets worse when stirred."

The barber didn't bother answering Sancho, in case his plain speaking gave away what he and the curate were trying so hard to conceal. With the same worry in mind the curate had asked the canon to ride on a little ahead so he could tell him the mystery of the man in the cage, along with other things that would entertain him. The canon agreed, and going on ahead with his servants, listened attentively to the account the curate gave him of Don Quixote's character, life, madness, and ways — describing briefly the beginning and origin of his craze, telling the whole story of his adventures up to his being confined in the cage, and outlining their plan to take him home to see if any cure might be found for his madness. The canon and his servants were astonished anew at Don Quixote's strange story, and when it was finished he said, "To tell the truth, señor curate, for my part I consider what they call books of chivalry to be harmful to the State. Though, led by idle and false taste, I've read the beginnings of almost all that have been printed, I could never manage to finish a single one, because they all seem more or less the same thing — one has nothing more in it than another. And in my opinion this sort of writing and composition is of the same species as the fables they call Milesian: nonsensical tales aimed solely at amusement and not instruction, the exact opposite of the apologue fables which both amuse and instruct. And even if amusement be the chief object of such books, I don't see how they can succeed when they're so full of monstrous nonsense. The enjoyment the mind feels must come from the beauty and harmony it perceives in what the eye or the imagination puts before it, and nothing with ugliness or disproportion about it can give pleasure. What beauty, then, or what proportion of the parts to the whole or of the whole to the parts, can there be in a book or fable in which a lad of sixteen cuts down a giant tall as a tower and makes two halves of him as if he were an almond cake? Or when they want to give us a picture of a battle, after telling us there are a million combatants on the enemy's side, the hero of the book is set against them, and we are obliged to believe, whether we like it or not, that this knight wins the victory by the single might of his strong arm. And then, what shall we say of how easily a queen or empress by birth will throw herself into the arms of some unknown wandering knight? What mind, unless wholly barbarous and uncultivated, can take pleasure in reading how a great tower full of knights sails over the sea like a ship with a fair wind, tonight in Lombardy and tomorrow morning in the land of Prester John of the Indies, or some other land Ptolemy never described nor Marco Polo saw? And if I'm told that the authors of such books write them as fiction, and so are not obliged to worry about niceties of truth, my reply is that fiction is better the more it resembles truth, and gives the more pleasure the more probability and possibility there is about it. Plots in fiction must be wedded to the understanding of the reader, and constructed in such a way that, reconciling impossibilities, smoothing over difficulties, keeping the mind alert, they may surprise, interest, divert, and entertain, so that wonder and delight may keep pace one with the other. All of this will fail in any writer who avoids verisimilitude and truth to nature, in which the perfection of writing lies. I've never yet seen a book of chivalry that puts together a coherent plot complete in all its parts, so that the middle agrees with the beginning and the end with the beginning and middle; on the contrary, they're constructed with such a tangle of limbs that it seems as if the authors were trying to produce a chimera or monster rather than a well-proportioned figure. And besides all this they are harsh in style, incredible in their feats, lascivious in their love-affairs, uncouth in their courtly speeches, prolix in their battles, silly in their arguments, absurd in their travels, and in short wanting in everything resembling intelligent art — for which reason they deserve to be banished from the Christian commonwealth as a worthless breed."

The curate listened attentively and felt the man was of sound understanding, and that there was good sense in what he said. So he told him that, being of the same opinion himself and bearing a grudge against books of chivalry, he had burned all of Don Quixote's — which were many — and gave him an account of the scrutiny he had made of them, of those he had condemned to the flames and those he had spared, all of which amused the canon a good deal. The canon added that though he had said so much in condemnation of these books, he did find one good thing in them: they afforded a gifted intellect a chance to display itself, since they offered a wide and spacious field over which the pen might range freely — describing shipwrecks, tempests, combats, battles, portraying a valiant captain with all the qualifications required to be one, showing him shrewd in foreseeing the enemy's wiles, eloquent in encouraging or restraining his soldiers, mature in counsel, swift in resolve, as bold in biding his time as in pressing the attack; now picturing some sad, tragic incident, now some joyful and unexpected event; here a beautiful lady, virtuous, wise, and modest; there a Christian knight, brave and gentle; here a lawless, barbarous braggart; there a courteous prince, gallant and gracious; setting forth the devotion and loyalty of vassals, the greatness and generosity of nobles. "Or again," he said, "the author may show himself as an astronomer, or a skilled cosmographer, or musician, or one versed in affairs of state, and at times he'll have the chance to appear as a magician if he likes. He can set forth the craftiness of Ulysses, the piety of Æneas, the valour of Achilles, the misfortunes of Hector, the treachery of Sinon, the friendship of Euryalus, the generosity of Alexander, the boldness of Cæsar, the clemency and truth of Trajan, the fidelity of Zopyrus, the wisdom of Cato — and in short all the qualities that go to make an illustrious man perfect, now uniting them in a single character, now distributing them among many; and if this be done with charm of style and ingenious invention, aiming at truth as much as possible, he will surely weave a web of bright and varied threads which, when finished, will display such perfection and beauty that it will attain the worthiest object any writing can seek — to give instruction and pleasure combined; for the unrestricted range of these books lets the author show his powers in the epic, lyric, tragic, or comic vein, and all the moods the sweet and winning arts of poetry and oratory are capable of, since the epic may be written in prose just as well as in verse."
